https://www.dw.com/en/eu-pulls-sponsorsh.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NzUl The conference took place at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius, but without several of its pre-planned backers [FILE: August 12, 2025] Image: Joko/picture alliance Advertisement The European Union on Thursday offered its reasons for withdrawing sponsorship for a disinformation event in Lithuania , following media reports claiming that it did so after pressure from the US government. The EU's foreign affairs division, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the governments of Canada and Lithuania all pulled their support from the event at short notice. Sponsors' logos on flyers and placards at the event were hastily covered over with paper strips. They withdrew participation in Disinfo2026 after pressure from the US State Department, according to reports in several media outlets, including the British newspaper The Guardian. What did the EU say about its decision? EU spokesperson Christian Wigand made no mention of the US or external pressure on Thursday but also did not repudiate the reports. "We were not comfortable with the framing of some of the discussions at the event," he told reporters in Brussels. "The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU," he said. He refused to discuss details of which discussions or what framing had perturbed the EEAS. He also would not comment on whether there had been talks with US officials on the matter. "I'm not commenting on diplomatic exchanges as a matter of principle," he said. What signs of potential controversy at Disinfo2026 were visible? While a number of the sessions planned on the event's website across two days at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius appeared to have the potential to perturb more sensitive members of Donald Trump's administration, the opening two sessions on Wednesday morning stood out. The opening of the conference was an interview with Kimberly Prost, a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC) , which has come under sustained and heavy fire from Trump and his administration during his second term. This was followed by an hourlong session entitled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back," using the acronym for Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference. One of the planned speakers was a former CIA officer. Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg.text: Image source, Reuters By Vitaly Shevchenko Â and Â Tom McArthur Published 10 October 2026, 11:29 BST Updated 2 hours ago Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, officials said. The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city on Saturday morning. At least 16 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel. He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting". Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed. "The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene. She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day. The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble. Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city." Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles . Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin Published 2 hours ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 18 hours ago Zelensky was quick to criticise Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin . Analysts view the deal as an attempt by the US president to allay domestic concerns about high fuel prices ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Zelensky wrote on social media on Saturday that Russian attacks on energy facilities in the capital, Kyiv, demonstrated Russia's "true intentions". "Russia's choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing. "Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different â signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking. And this needs to be corrected." Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on. On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region. The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv. The number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% , external in the first eight months of this year, according to the UN. Russia has also stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches, a strategy it has undertaken in previous years. Kyiv has repeatedly accused it of targeting Ukraine's civilian population, which Moscow denies. For its part, Ukraine has increasingly adopted a policy of striking infrastructure often deep inside Russia that is crucial to its economy, including several oil refineries and terminals. Several strikes on data centres owned by Yandex have left the tech giant struggling to maintain services. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at curtailing revenue streams for Russia's war machine.
